0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

This superscription, referring to events described in 2 Samuel 11:1–12:25, describes sexual relations in a polite way by using the phrase **had gone in to**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [he had slept with Bathsheba]

1.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to all the ways you are faithful to your covenant]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **compassions** and **transgressions**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [of ways you care for me, forgive all the ways I have sinned against you]

David is speaking of his **transgressions** as if they were words written in ink on a scroll that God could **wipe away** to erase them and make them disappear. The basic idea is that David wants God to regard his transgressions as if they had never occurred; that is, he wants God to forgive him for committing them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [completely forgive my transgressions]

2.note: The expressions **Make great** and **wash me** together express a single idea. The expression **Make great** tells in what way David wants God to **wash**him. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Wash me thoroughly to cleanse me of my sin] or [Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, yes, cleanse me from my sin]

This could mean (both meanings may be present): (1) that David is speaking of his **iniquity** or **sin** as if it were actually dirt or a stain that God could **wash** off of him in order to **cleanse** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Completely take away my iniquity, yes, remove all of my sin] or (2) that David is speaking as if his **iniquity** or **sin** had made him ritually unclean and so unable to participate in the worship of God until he became ritually clean again through ceremonial washing. Alternate translation: [Take away all of my iniquity to make me acceptable to you again so that I can worship you freely]

3.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an admission. Alternate translation: [Indeed,] or [Admittedly,]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I know** already includes this meaning. He is doing that because he is confronting himself with the fact of his **transgressions**. Alternate translation: [I know very well that I have committed transgressions]

David is speaking of his **sin** as if it were actually an object that was **always before** him or in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I am always conscious of my sin]

4.note: David is repeating the pronoun **you** for emphasis. If your language can repeat pronouns for emphasis, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [You are the only one I have sinned against]

David is saying **only** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [You are the one I have essentially sinned against]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is evil]
Here, **eyes** represents “perspective.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your perspective]

5.note: David is using the term **Behold** to focus attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, here and in the next verse.

David does not mean that his **mother conceived** him as the result of a sinful act. Instead, he means that as a human being, he has been characterized by **iniquity** and **sin** for his entire life. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I have been iniquitous since I was born; indeed, I have been sinful from the time my mother conceived me]

The expression **was born** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I was in iniquity when my mother gave birth to me; indeed, I was in sin when my mother conceived me]

6.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [trustworthiness] or [integrity]
Here the **kidneys** represents a person’s motives and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in a person’s motives]

The expression **closed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in the place that people close up]

David is using the verbal form **closed**, which functions here as an adjective, as a noun to mean a certain place. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **place**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [in my inner being]

7.note: David is speaking as if he wanted God to perform the ceremony that the law of Moses describes in Numbers 19:18, in which a ceremonially clean person would dip a **hyssop** branch in water and sprinkle water with it to **purify** a person or place that had become ritually unclean. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The UST models one way to do that.

The term **hyssop** describes a leafy plant, an herb that was common in Israel. Its large and numerous leaves made it ideal for use in sprinkling, especially in ceremonial contexts. If your language does not have a word for this plant, consider using a general expression. Alternate translation: [with leafy branches]

As in verse 2, David is speaking of his sin as if it were dirt that God could **wash** off of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar image in verse 2. Alternate translation: [May you take away my sin]

David is speaking as if he would become bright white in color if God were to wash him. He is using the uniform whiteness of newly fallen snow to represent complete purity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that I may be purer than snow]

8.note: David is using the expression **joy and gladness** to represent things that God would say to him that would make him feel those emotions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Make me hear things that will cause me to feel joy and gladness] or [Say things to me that will make me feel joy and gladness]

David means specifically that he wants God to tell him that he has forgiven him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Assure me that you have forgiven me, that I may feel joy and gladness]

The terms **joy** and **gladness** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great joy]

David is using one part of himself, his **bones**, to mean all of him in the act of being **crushed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may I, whom you have crushed, rejoice]

David is speaking as if God had actually **crushed** him by convicting him of his sin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may I, whom you have deeply convicted of sin, rejoice]

9.note: David is speaking as if he wanted God to position his **face** so that it would not be visible from the place where his **sins** were. Effectively this means that he wants God not to look at his sins. However, he does not mean that he wants God to leave his sins in place but not regard them. He wants God to make his sins nowhere to be seen; that is, he wants God to forgive the sins so that it is as if he had not committed them. Alternate translation: [Make my sins nowhere to be seen]
See how you translated the same image in verse 1. Alternate translation: [and forgive all of my iniquities]

10.note: Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts or motives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Give me a new capacity for pure thoughts] or [Give me a new capacity for right motives]

The expression **established** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and renew a steadfast spirit within me]

Here a person’s **spirit** represents his attitude, in this case, one of determination. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and enable me once again to be steadfastly determined to obey you]

11.note: Here God’s **face** represents his “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [May you not cast me away from your presence]

David is speaking as if God might actually **cast** or throw him away from his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May you not banish me from your presence]

David is using the possessive form to describe how God’s **Spirit** is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and may you not take your Holy Spirit from me]

12.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **joy** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Make me joyful again that you have saved me]

David is speaking as if he wanted God to use a **willing spirit** like a cane or walking stick to **support** him, that is, to keep him from falling down. Within this image, falling down represents disobeying and sinning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to keep me from sinning, make me willing to obey you]

13.note: David is speaking of the manners in which God wants people to live as if they were **ways** or paths that people would be walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how you want people to live]

David is speaking as if **sinners** had actually gone to some place away from God from which they would **return** to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that sinners may repent]

14.note: Here, **blood** represents “bloodguiltiness,” that is, legal liability to punishment by death for murdering another person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the death penalty I deserve for killing someone]

David is repeating the word **God** to emphasize that the basis of his plea is the merciful, saving character of God. If your language can repeat words for emphasis, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the emphasis. Alternate translation: [you who are God my Savior]

David is using one part of himself, his **tongue**, to mean all of him in the act of singing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may I sing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about how righteous you are]

15.note: David is not asking God physically to **open** his **lips**. He means that he wants God to do something (forgive and restore him, as he has asked) that will cause him to open his lips and declare God’s praise with his mouth. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Do this, Lord, so that I may open my lips]

Here David’s **lips** represent him speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [give me something to speak about]

David is using one part of himself, his **mouth**, to mean all of him in the act of praising God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that I may declare your praise]

16.note: Here the word **For** does not introduce a reason for what immediately precedes. Instead, it introduces a general explanation for what David has been asking throughout this psalm. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]

David means specifically that God does not want a **sacrifice** and that God does not **accept a burnt offering** as the grounds on which to pardon someone who has committed murder. (The law of Moses provides for no such sacrifice.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you do not delight in sacrifice in cases of murder … you do not accept a burnt offering to pardon a murderer]

17.note: David is using this possessive form not to describe **sacrifices** that **God** makes but sacrifices that God wants and accepts. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The sacrifices that God wants] or [The sacrifices that God accepts]

The expression **broken** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [are a spirit that has broken]

David is speaking as if a person’s **spirit** were actually an object that could be **broken**. The image is of something that is broken so that it has fallen down in pieces, with lowliness representing humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are a humble spirit]
As in verse 10, here a person’s **spirit** represents his attitude. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are a humble attitude]

The expressions **broken** and **crushed** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [A heart that an awareness of the seriousness of sin has broken and crushed]

The terms **broken** and **crushed** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [A completely broken heart] or [A heart that an awareness of the seriousness of sin has completely broken]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s inner being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A person who is deeply humbled by an awareness of the seriousness of his sin]

18.note: David is using Mount **Zion**, the location of the Israelite capital city of Jerusalem, to represent the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

The noun that the ULT translates as **acceptance** here comes from the same root as the verb that it translates as “accept” in verse 16. However, the perspective is broader here. David is not asking God to **Do good to Zion** based on God’s **acceptance** of him personally as a penitent and forgiven sinner. Instead, he is asking that all of the people of Israel would experience God’s renewed favor now that he, as their king, has repented. Your language may have a term that you can use in your translation to indicate this. Alternate translation: [in your favor]

David is speaking as if **Jerusalem** did not have **walls**, and he wanted God to **build** some for the city. He is using Jerusalem to represent the people of Israel and walls to represent their protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [strengthen the defenses of Israel] or [strongly protect us Israelites]

19.note: David is using the possessive form to describe **sacrifices** that are characterized by the **righteousness** of those offering them. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [rightly offered sacrifices]

David is using the adjective **whole** as a noun to mean a certain kind of sacrifice. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **one**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a burnt offering and a wholly consumed sacrifice]

Together, the expressions **a burnt offering** and **a whole one** express a single idea. The word **whole** tells to what extent this **offering** would be **burnt**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [a wholly burnt offering]

David is not referring to a specific wholly burnt offering. He means such offerings in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [wholly burnt offerings]

Here David is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Then people will offer bulls] or [Then bulls will be offered]
